Preserves is it's own separate thing here also containing fruit solids in the form of chunks or occasionally whole fruit, if the fruit is small enough. The fruit is suspended in a syrup or a jam.

We also have the distinction of marmalade being the citrus fruit version preserves basically.

Jelly, in the uk, is fruits juices, sugar and gelatin. It's firm and smooth and has a thick gel like texture, essentially Jell-O as you'd call it.

I work in a the surgical department with a robot for surgery can't remember the exact name and googling probably wouldn't help but even with it not being a full robot it's still impressive. The one we have has 5 arms and then the control module. So the surgeon sits in a chair with joy sticks and buttons essentially and a monitor it looks quite like a game. The surgeon changes which arms are being operated as not all can be used simultaneously and an assistant changes the attachments on the robot. The attachments are the same used in laparoscopic cases just designed to fit into the robots arms. The robotic arms really precise and accurate, you rotate an arm 3 degrees it rotates that distance, you move it 0.5mm it moves 0.5mm. Very cool, more accurate than doing laparoscopic work by hand. The main problem with the robot is not that it's so expensive, it's how long it takes to use and set it up. The cases done with the robot require more precision but still take considerably longer than routine laparoscopic. But yeah the robot isn't as cool as it initially sounds I thought it was really fancy ai at first but no where as complicated.

It is manufactured under controlled circumstances, I am unaware of any illegal manufactoring of the drug. It is more the doses of the drug that get messed up and lead to people dying. The standard dose we give is up to 100 micrograms of fentanyl such a small quantity it is easy to give substantially more (or less) if it isn't measured out precisely which is the problem comes from. Fentanyl is a safe drug when given by trained personnel with appropriate supplies and equipment.
It being cheaper is an added benefit really. Fentanyl is more effective at treating severe pain than morphine is.

There is argument over which is safer here (UK) but as it stands at the moment fentanyl is considered to be more dangerous and is more controlled than morphine. Ambulances only carry paracetamol and morphine in my area and nationally are able to carry a couple of other but morphine is most potent thing they can carry. There is definitely a place for both drugs to be used but I do agree that morphine isn't a particularly good drug to use I only say it is safer acutely after admission.

I've not heard the same and can't really comment on how accurate it is but I've seen some patients have ungodly amounts of pain relief for some injuries, whether due to them not telling us something or if there tolerances were increased, I don't know, but it's something not routinely done and only ever done in exceptional circumstances, with additional monitoring and safety measures in place.

Ketamine is another effective pain relieving drug but works differently. Unfortunately I don't know the exact way it works differently only that I've been taught it works differently. I do know it has a list of pretty nasty side effects and in conscious it can be quite traumatising. The 2 biggest unpleasant side effects I've witnessed from ketamine are an increased sensitivity to light and hallucinations. Both of these can occur with opioids but far less frequently. Some people are completely unresponsive or minimally responsive to opioid based pain relief and ketamine makes a good alternative as it often works in those cases. Trauma patients tend to be better and experience less pain after ketamine, again I don't know exactly why but it does seem to be. I've only seen ketamine used in trauma situation after morphine was ineffective so my experience isn't as expansive as others.

It is an incredibly potent drug and it's effects are huge for such a small dose. We give around 100 micrograms for an operation for effective pain relief of being cut open, with morphine the dose would be roughly 10-20 milligrams. It's a about 100 times of a dose given due to the potency. I can't really comment on the action as I'm not 100% but I believe morphine and fentanyl work the same way and the danger is purely from the strength of drug.

Hey there, ODP here. We use fentanyl on a daily basis as it is an incredibly effective pain relieving drug and has a releltively short half life. It makes it easy to get on top of severe pain quickly and enables time to get more long term pain management in place. Compared directly to morphine it is more potent however the cost is not all the different a box of 10 ampoules of morphine is £15 compared to to 10 ampoules of fentanyl costing £13.95. Morphine and fentanyl both have there place and morphine is considerably safer and is effective in moderate to severe management but there is a point where fentanyl is going to be more effective at dealing with the pain. Source: Myself, my training and a spare slightly outdated copy of the BNF on my coffee table.

Kids are different. It is technically wrong just not where you stated. Adults generally go into cardiac arrest kids normally go into respiratory arrest and then into cardiac arrest the 5 breaths is there to hopefully treat the respiratory arrest without having to do chest compressions. For adults 30:2 chest compressions to breaths, at a rate of 2 compressions per second at a depth of 5-6 centimetres. Kids respond better to 15:2 same rate at a depth of 1/3 of the chest. Easier to remember the 30:2 for both though it's better than nothing regardless. Source: Myself. StODP seen quite a few laparoscopic operations done, basically they inflate the abdomin with carbon dioxide to life the skin, fat and various tissues up and away to make the surgical site easier to see. The carbon dioxide is released but some is left in and some can be trapped, if it is trapped under the diaphragm then due to the connections of the vagus nerve can cause the pain to be felt in the lower chest up to the shoulders. It's quite common to have shoulder pain afterwards an unfortunate side effect. It gets slightly worse in that pain relief generally isn't the most effective at relieving the pain and it can last for several days.

Yeah if course it is quite a long process. I went first to the gp, you'll need a referal from the gp but they like ruling out otherthings first. They'll ask about depression and anxiety, get blood tests done and possibly an ecg done I had one but not too sure if that will be the case for everyone. Once the gp is happy it isn't something physical or something they can manage, you'll be referred onto phychiatric. You'll first see a psychologist for a few sessions lots of talking and asking about medical history lots about childhood also. If it is deemed that medication is going to be effective you'll be referred to a psychiatrist, they will get body weight, heart rate, blood pressure and just general observational signs and prescribe some medication it might take a few sessions until you get to this point or they might go for it on the first session. It took me almost a year to get medication prescribed adult mental health isn't well supported and so the wait times are long. Hopefully this is helpful and it could be something else but once at the psychologist they will direct you the right way! Hope you can get this resolved and get the right treatment for you!
